title: Cross and crucifix
hook: an empty cross, or Christ on it: churches choose differently

segments.voice: Yesterday, candles, and a small flame that keeps going after you've walked out the door. Your line was a prayer left burning. Who did you leave a light for? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-two.

On a jeweler's tray, two silver necklaces. Same chain, same size, same shape. One is a plain cross: two bars, nothing else. The other carries a tiny figure, arms stretched wide, head bowed. Now go into a church on one corner, and the big cross above the altar has that figure on it. Cross the street to another church, and the cross on the wall is bare wood. Nobody in either building forgot anything. Each one chose. And the two choices turn out to be saying the same sentence, with the stress on different words. Today: cross and crucifix.
screen: `ONE CHURCH: A FIGURE. ONE CHURCH: BARE WOOD.`

segments.voice: First, the plain difference. A crucifix is a cross with the figure of Christ on it. A cross, on its own, is the shape with nobody on it. Both point at the same death: an execution, which the letter to the Hebrews places outside the city gate. That's the strange thing hiding in plain sight. An instrument of death ended up on necklaces and steeples. Paul wrote to the Galatians: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." Glory, in the cross. Next, the crucifix. Catholic churches keep one on or near the altar, and Orthodox Christians often use crosses with Christ painted on them, like an icon. Paul wrote to the church in Corinth: "For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified." Some who pray before a crucifix say it keeps the cost in view: this happened to a real body, with real nails, and it isn't tidied away. Then the empty cross. In other churches, Protestant ones especially, the cross is bare. That isn't a cross with something missing. To those who choose it, the emptiness is the message. In Matthew's Gospel, the women come to the tomb at dawn, and the angel tells them: "He is not here: for he is risen, as he said." The bare cross points to that morning. Last, put them side by side. Churches with a crucifix still sing about the empty tomb. Churches with a bare cross still read the story of the nails. So the two shapes aren't two beliefs. They're one story, told with the weight on a different moment. One holds the death in view. The other holds the morning after. In both kinds of church, the whole sentence gets said: he died, and he rose.
screen: `AN INSTRUMENT OF DEATH, WORN ON A CHAIN.`
`THE BARE CROSS: HE IS NOT HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a cross. Settle, and breathe. If there's one near you, a necklace, a picture on a wall, a steeple out the window, look at it. If not, the screen has one. First, just notice: is it empty, or does it carry a figure? Then let your eyes move slowly, the upright beam, the crossbeam, the place where the two meet. Stay with whichever kind you have. If it's a crucifix, notice the arms. If it's bare, notice the space. If you pray, you can pray in the words your own church uses before a cross. If you don't, simply look, and let it be a shape that carries a story. The bell holds the time.
Cross and crucifix. The bare shape, and the shape with Christ on it: two ways of showing one story.
Your line: he died, he rose. Today, every time you pass a cross, on a church, a necklace, a roadside, notice which kind it is: empty, or not. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Catholic churches keep a crucifix on or near the altar, Orthodox churches often use crosses with Christ painted on them, and Protestant churches often display a plain cross; Christians of every kind may wear either on a chain.

notes: Editor pass: replaced 'Rome's way of killing, outside the city walls' with the Hebrews 'outside the city gate' wording (paraphrase cited), dropped 'already' before Paul's Galatians line, and softened the closing claim about what Christians across churches say.
Review picks up day 1361 (Candles) from the index; its script was not on disk when this was written.

'Catholic churches keep one [a crucifix] on or near the altar' reflects Roman Catholic liturgical norms; confirm wording. Some Lutheran and Anglican churches also use crucifixes; not mentioned to keep the lesson simple.
'Orthodox Christians often use crosses with Christ painted on them, like an icon' and 'Protestant ones especially' for bare crosses: deliberately unquantified; confirm fair.
'Outside the city walls' leans on Hebrews 13:12 ('without the gate') and John 19:20 (near the city); confirm.
Original: σταυρός, pronunciation given as stow-ROSS; confirm the transliteration preferred for this path.
